chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
title: Booker Washington, the Memphis pit drummer who inspired him
summary: Crawford explains that Booker Washington at the Palace Theater on Beale Street, with his stick tricks, made him want to be a drummer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Now, I wanted to -- before we go to
New York, I wanted to go back some and deal with your earlier life as a drummer.
Oh, I'd like to tell you something.

Stanley, my inspiration to become a drummer was a fellow who inspired me to no end, the utmost in sensational drumming, was a drummer by the name of Booker Washington at the Palace Theater. He was in the pit, only had about seven, eight pieces, but my aunt used to take me to the Palace Theater once a week so I could see this drummer. Boy, that man, wow, who played the Palace Theater -- Butterbeans and Susie, (inaudible) Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, all those type of people.
Well, how was the theater built? What did it look like?
Oh, the Palace Theater on Beale Street? It was just a Negro theater, you know, and just -- four walls and a roof over it.
I can't remember, can't recall right now, but apparently it was for cheap prices for admittance.
You remember how much it cost to get in?
Oh, about 35 or something like that, and I think that may have been tops. But this drummer had sticks on -- rolling around in his fingers like wheels,

throwing them in the air, and I always said in the present day that no drummer can play drums with the sticks in the air, but it happened then with this fellow in Memphis. Booker Washington, later on he died. He went to New Orleans, then came back to Memphis, and then he went to Chicago, and he passed there from pneumonia or tuberculosis.
